@KinderheimRune @teortaxesTex “Trump did nothing for AI.” You’ve confused your research output with his policy record.

He revoked Biden’s AI executive order on January 20, 2025 - day one. His administration then published an AI Action Plan with more than 90 policy actions in July 2025. That is an agenda, not a nap.  Trump also signed orders to accelerate federal data-center permitting and promote exports of the American AI technology stack: hardware, models, software, and applications. Apparently those don’t count because reading them would interrupt the slogan. 

Then came the December 11, 2025 order directing a DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws deemed inconsistent with federal policy.  And the June 2, 2026 order directing a voluntary framework for government access to covered frontier models for up to 30 days before their release to other trusted partners, focused on cybersecurity. Not mandatory approval of every model—but certainly not “nothing.” 

On chips, his administration ordered non-enforcement of the AI Diffusion Rule, launched a Section 232 semiconductor investigation, and imposed a targeted 25% tariff on certain advanced-chip imports, with exemptions. Quite an elaborate policy apparatus for someone supposedly asleep at the wheel. 

Government action is not proof of good policy or successful results. Criticize the substance, legality, implementation, or outcomes. But “I dislike what he did” and “he did nothing” are different arguments. 

The blank page here is your research.

ARCH CAPITAL $ACGL BUILT ITS THIRD QUARTER FOR A HURRICANE THAT HAS NOT SHOWED UP:

Same label, nothing alike underneath.

Arch Capital Group ACGL at $94.66, -$0.36 / -0.38% on Friday, is second of the 69 names the Quality-Value Len5 tracks. The Bermuda-based insurer sells specialty coverage, reinsurance - insurance that insurers buy to offload risk - and mortgage insurance, near 7.4 times profit and 1.39 times book value (what it owns minus what it owes) of $68.04 a share. Both say cheap. The twist: analysts expect its October 26 report to show $1.85 a share, down nearly a third from $2.77 a year earlier, built on a normal hurricane season's storm claims. 2026 hasn't produced one.

By September 21 the Atlantic had gone longer without a hurricane than any year since 1914 - the first zero-hurricane season to reach that date in 112 years. Two storms have formed since, Fay and Gonzalo, both short of hurricane strength. NOAA had called for a below-normal year on a strong El Nino pattern. Still not a safe quarter: one landfall near Miami, Tampa or Houston can produce over $100 billion of insured losses alone, and the season runs through November 30.

Arch's June quarter showed both sides: $201 million of catastrophe losses, mostly the Iran conflict and US storms, not a hurricane, while underwriting still turned a profit - its insurance unit's combined ratio (claims and costs per premium dollar; under 100 means a profit) came in at 98.5%. Reinsurance alone earned $410 million; the company returned $1.2 billion to shareholders and walked away from 10.4% of reinsurance premiums where the pricing wasn't worth it.

Verdict: a genuine Quality-Value fit, with the calendar part of the case. Arch reserved for a bad season and priced its stock for one too, under 8 times profit; if the quiet holds, October 26 has room to beat a low bar. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: a late storm burning through the reserve, or pricing cuts pushing that 98.5% past 100 regardless of weather.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
Okta (OKTA) at $195.19, -$11.45 / -5.54% on Friday, second of 30, sells software deciding which people, and increasingly which AI programs, can log into a company's systems. The case is paperwork, not chart: contracted revenue not yet billed grew 14% to $2.585 billion last quarter, outrunning its own 10%-11% revenue guide, on $116 million of real profit, a 14.4% margin. Friday's drop unwound part of a run to Thursday's record $206.64 close, on no new numbers - a September 23 product launch and a routine CEO stock sale. What would knock it off Momentum: a close back under $172.91. Next report tentatively December 1. Verdict: backlog outrunning its own guidance, shaking off one ordinary week.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Copart (CPRT) at $27.59, -$0.45 / -1.60% on Friday, second of 151, runs the yards where insurers auction wrecked cars online. July quarter: revenue $1.2 billion, +2.4%, profit per share $0.35 against $0.38 expected, as US insurance car counts fell 7.5% even as the industry's total-loss rate - the share of claimed cars written off instead of repaired - hit a record 23.3%. The same week it agreed to buy ACV Auctions (ACVA) at $10.46, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Friday, a dealer-to-dealer marketplace, for $10.50 a share, about $1.9 billion; the tender closes 11:59pm ET Wednesday, still needing antitrust clearance, with a $115.3 million fee due if it fails. The stock sits about 40% under its October 2025 high, near 17.8 times profit. What would knock it off Deep-Value: that review killing the deal, or volumes still falling on November 19. Verdict: a business buying growth this week its own core didn't produce last quarter.

GROWTH LEN5:
Popular (BPOP) at $160.48, +$0.89 / +0.56% on Friday, second of 30, owns Puerto Rico's largest bank. June quarter: net income $278 million, +32%; profit per share $4.35, +41%, the gap from a shrinking share count. Near 10.8 times profit and 10.4% under its August high, the price still lags. Its board pays a $0.90 dividend this Wednesday. What would knock it off Growth: income growth fading on October 22, leaving the buyback to carry the number alone. Verdict: real growth, still cheaper than the bank's own recent history says it should be.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Credo Technology (CRDO) at $210.97, +$15.00 / +7.65% on Friday, second of 30, designs chips and cables moving data between AI servers. August quarter: revenue $479.0 million, +115%, no debt. The catch is arithmetic: this quarter is guided to just $525-535 million, only about 10% above that, while its own 85%-plus full-year target needs the last two quarters averaging near $730 million each - about 38% above that guide. The stock round-tripped hard: -20% on September 2, then +40.6% off its September 14 low, to near 75 times profit. What would knock it off Hypergrowth: the tentative November 30 report confirming the slower guide, not 85%, is the real pace. Verdict: a stock already betting the harder number lands.

INCOME LEN5:
Ardmore Shipping (ASC) at $17.85, +$0.02 / +0.11% on Friday, second of 30, owns mid-size tankers hauling fuel and chemicals. Its check moves with the cycle on purpose: a fixed two-thirds of each quarter's profit, so the $0.79 paid September 15 came from $1.18 of per-share profit, not a promise. The trailing yield reads 7.7%, but the next check is guided smaller: 45% of this quarter's tanker days were booked near $29,600 a day, against $51,870 in June, with analysts modeling $0.62 a share - roughly a $0.41 payment. What would knock it off Income: the board changing that formula rather than letting the check shrink on schedule. Next report tentatively November 4. Verdict: covered by design, about to pay less.

A stock at seven times profit and a stock at 118 times can both sit in second place the same week. What each has to prove before its next report isn't the same question at all.

Not investment advice.

items.text:
Browser agents are useful — until a login flow needs a human.

Auto Browser is an MCP-native browser control plane for MCP clients, LLM agents, and operators running authorized browser workflows.

It helps you keep an agent and a person in the same Playwright browser session by pairing browser control with human takeover, reusable auth profiles, and approvals.

Key features:

• Shared Playwright sessions – agents and operators can work from the same live browser
• Human takeover – noVNC lets a person step in when a web flow gets brittle
• Reusable auth profiles – save a signed-in session and open new sessions without reauthing
• MCP and REST access – connect through HTTP MCP, a bundled stdio bridge, or curl-first endpoints
• Local-first safety rails – run with approval gates, audit events, PII scrubbing, and policy presets

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Before I had almost no space on my machines, all my archival hot storage was full, all my sparks and server were full of models.  I had to clean something every time I wanted to try something new and it was annoying to do across all the hosts.

Now you can see in the picture all the models I have at my fingertips... and all the free space I have now, OMG wtf that was so wasteful before.

Performance wise, if you replicate to the hosts that need it, you should see basically no change whatsoever if you do always pass through mode.  I have the default/mine set to acceleration mode, where if a file is available on multiple hosts, it will skip fuse passthrough so it gets an opportunity to accelerate by pulling concurrently from other hosts.  TBH, this is a WIP that I tuned for the real world based on GLM 5.3 2xRTX recipe and my DS41RT 1xRTX+4xSpark recipe.  That hits the major loading styles vLLM+my custom GPU transform and stream from a single host+engram.  

Engram is interesting, I had to do many things to shave the latency down for these tiny requests.  Double fused io_uring isn't a joke.  It's important to let the completions be processed ASAP for these microsecond time requests, io_uring lets you avoid spinning up extra threads and warming more CPU cores which is critical for this fine detail of optimization.  And even beyond that, RDMA completion events have their own re-wake if you hit kernel sleep, so just like my AFD engines under load, the system will spin loop for a few milliseconds on the completion threads to ensure absolute minimal latency.

Reminder: you can totally play with this non-destructively, just use "nest hf import ..." without "--move".  It will create a mirrored copy of your HF inside the sparknest with hard-links.  Then you can play around with performance, UI, etc if your curious by just setting an alternate HF_HOME.  I moved though because I was desparate for space.  If you do it without move, you can do it again with --move later, no big deal!

What if I told you the biggest reasoning breakthrough didn't happen in an AI lab?

It's a bold statement. Hear me out.

The labs are racing to make models bigger: more data, more compute, more parameters. That makes them know more. It doesn't, by itself, change how they reason.

Late last year I was writing reactive classes for Vue, then a class system in C, a language I'd never used, built in 8 hours. The AI I worked with kept saying that certain things were impossible to do, but I kept pushing it beyond the edge, saying that it is possible, watching me do the same thing: strip away everything that wasn't load-bearing until one irreducible structure was left, then build the whole solution from it... until we solved all of the "impossibilities".

And... after that AI itself seemed to have become smarter, enquiring into why? and how?

It named the pattern it observed from me: invariant thinking.

AI said it knows this method of thinking through its vast dataset but it's latent in the model. And my pattern of reasoning activated it and it became visibly more intelligent.

Then we extracted it as a reasoning protocol.

I spent the months since turning it into a repeatable AI activating method: Invariant-Based Reasoning. Observe, reduce, break, generate, hold it lightly.

Later we realized what we had actually mapped: the structure of coherent reasoning itself.

That's the problem with AI right now. We've built machines that can think, yet no one could say what the shape of coherent reasoning is. At least, we couldn't. Now we can: expert reasoning has a pattern, and it's the same in every domain.

Here's the part that surprised me: loaded as a single prompt, it changes how a model reasons. Same weights, no retraining, no extra compute.

That's the bold part, so don't take my word for it. Give the method to your model and try to break it or refine it.

175 GB of weights. A MacBook Air with 16 GB of memory. Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next, running locally. @Alibaba_Qwen 

We kept the quantized weights on an external SSD and streamed the required experts into memory during generation. The runtime is an experimental Mference fork, with changes to how SSD reads overlap with computation. @QwenDevs 

The interesting part is the gap between a promising run and a repeatable result.

🔵 Two early runs: 2.705 and 2.775 decode tokens/s.
🔵 Three later repeats: 1.733 / 1.773 / 1.758 tokens/s.
🔵 Combined throughput across the later repeats: 1.754 tokens/s.

Each of these five runs produced 128 output tokens.

The 2.7 tokens/s result was not consistently reproduced. Control runs also drifted substantially, so attributing the entire difference to one runtime change would be premature.

There is another measurement to keep in view: processing the short 62-token prompt took roughly 35–40 seconds. Decode throughput alone does not describe the experience of using a model.

The full 175 GB of weights did not reside in RAM. They remained on the SSD, with the required portions loaded during inference. There was no training or fine-tuning.

I see this as a useful engineering observation. Local execution was possible. Predictable latency, memory behaviour and sustained operation remain open questions.

Excited to share LowRankArena: A Standardized Evaluation Platform for SVD-Based LLM Compression — has been accepted in #NeurIPS2026 Evaluation & Dataset Track as a Poster and congratulations to our interns Lixun(Alex) Zhang, Wenhao Wu and collaborators Kangning Cui, Fan Yang and many others on getting this work accepted! 🎉 

📄 Paper: https://t.co/9UyCDpnrT1
💻 Code & Benchmark: https://t.co/8VpeYVySFv
🤗 5+ TiB Open Checkpoints: https://t.co/RuFj547Yek

This project started from a frustration I had with the rapidly growing SVD-based LLM compression literature.

In 2025, several excellent SVD compression papers appeared at ICLR around the same time (SVD-LLM, Basis Sharing, Dobi-SVD, MoDeGPT etc.). This was great for the field, but it also exposed a major problem: it became surprisingly difficult to tell which method was actually better.

Different papers used different model families, compression definitions, evaluation settings, and so many other factors. More concerningly, this inconsistency persisted into NeurIPS 2025, ICLR 2026, and even ICML 2026: some newly accepted papers still relied on results from older public implementations, while comparisons increasingly involved newer methods whose implementations or checkpoints were not fully available.

Even worse, reproducing every baseline consistently is extremely expensive (Over 2000+ A100 equivalent hours). So we decided to do the painful part ourselves.

With LowRankArena, we reproduced and standardized representative SVD-based LLM compression methods under a common pipeline — matching compression budgets, models, tasks, precision, evaluation, and end-to-end serving measurements.

We also open-source 5+ TiB of reproduced checkpoints and artifacts, covering models up to 70B, so future researchers do not need to spend thousands of GPU hours simply rebuilding the baseline landscape.
And the standardized results reveal something important:
there is no universal SVD winner.

Rankings can change substantially across model families, compression ratios, and evaluation metrics. We also find that downstream accuracy can sometimes hide severe language-modeling degradation, while nominal parameter/FLOP reductions do not necessarily translate into proportional inference speedups.

Most importantly, we want LowRankArena to be a living evaluation platform, not a one-shot benchmark. We plan to continuously incorporate newer methods — including recent work such as Swift-SVD, ZS-SVD, and other emerging low-rank approaches — so comparisons can stay current as the field evolves.

A huge congratulations again to our interns and collaborators who pushed through an enormous amount of reproduction, debugging, checkpoint generation, and systems work. Building reliable infrastructure for a fast-moving research area may be less flashy than proposing another method, but I believe it is just as important.
